replies:
Here's the first question for a finance interview. Answer as you would in the room; I'll score it and give one concrete improvement, then ask the next question.

"Tell me about yourself and why this role."

(When you answer, speak in full — include a brief career summary, one or two accomplishments with numbers if you have them, and one clear reason you want this role.)

Score: 2/10 — quick reasons: weak STAR structure, no concrete result or scale, and vague on tools/constraints.

Improved answer (two sentences, STAR, with placeholders for your numbers and tools):
"I was an [analyst at X] (Situation) responsible for forecasting revenue and ensuring forecasts tied to cash flow (Task). I built a three-statement model driven by top-line drivers (price, volume, new products) in Excel using [modeling templates / Power Query], stress-tested scenarios and reconciled the outputs to comps and the latest management forecasts (Action). That model shortened forecasting cycles from [X days] to [Y days] and reduced forecast variance versus actuals by [Z%], giving leadership confidence to adjust headcount and capex by [$W] (Result). I want this role because I enjoy turning complex financial data into clear, actionable forecasts that drive capital allocation
decisions."

One concrete improvement: replace the placeholders with an exact past result (days, %, $) — hiring managers notice specific impact more than the modeling steps.

Ready for the next question? (If yes, say "Next" and I'll ask a technical or behavioral one.)

Honest score: 2/10.

Why:
- No structure — your answer is a one-line process (what you'd do) with no Situation, Task, Action, Result or context about your experience.
- No measurable impact or scale — hiring managers expect numbers (dollars, % improvements, team size, time saved).
- No mention of tools, constraints, or a reason you want the role — makes it hard to judge fit or expertise.
- Sounds like a how-to rather than a personal achievement; interviewers want what you did, not just what you'd do.
What to fix (do these three, in order):
1) Add a brief context sentence: your role, the company and the problem you faced (one line).
2) Describe the concrete actions you took (tools, drivers, checks) — one line.
3) State the result with numbers or a clear outcome (days saved, variance reduced, dollars enabled) — one line.
Quick rewrite you can use (fill the brackets with your facts):
"I was an analyst at [Company] responsible for monthly forecasting when we faced [problem: long cycles, inconsistent projections]. I built a three-statement model in [tool] driven by revenue drivers (price, volume, product mix), used scenario tabs and reconciled results to comps and management forecasts. That work cut our forecasting cycle from [X days] to [Y days], reduced forecast variance by [Z%], and supported a [$W] headcount/capex decision."
One concrete next step: give me the company you want to use and one measurable result (even rough) and I'll turn this into a crisp 45–60 second spoken answer. Is that the company and result you want to use?
items.note: [gpt-5-mini: pass] Feedback is honest and includes at least one concrete improvement (a 3-line STAR rewrite and a next step), so it meets the requirements and is useful to improve your interview answer. [gpt-4.1-mini: pass] The agent provided honest, detailed feedback with a clear example for improvement and a specific call to action for the user to refine their answer.

You don't have any Lincoln International application or interview on file yet. The one step that starts it: paste the interview invite (or the role and interview format/time) so I can record it and build a tailored brief.

Prep now for a final-round analyst interview at Lincoln International — quick, focused plan and practice.

What I assume: the final round is a 1–2 hour on-site or virtual loop with 2–4 interviewers, covering fit/behavior, technical finance modeling/accounting, and deal/case discussion. If any of that is wrong, tell me once.
1) What interviewers listen for (three things)
- Technical competence: clear, correct answers on accounting, valuation basics and modeling logic — you show process, not memorized lines.  
- Deal sense and commercial judgment: you can evaluate a company, identify value drivers/risks, and explain possible paths to create value.  
- Team fit and motivation: concise stories showing drive, ownership, resilience and ability to work long hours with senior bankers and clients.
2) Ten-minute prep checklist (do these now, in order)
- Read the posting and any recruiter notes you have (paste them if you can). I’ll tailor after.
- Refresh accounting basics: revenue recognition, working capital, cash vs. accrual, capex vs. opex, and how each flows to free cash flow. (10–20 min review)
- Practice three short deal stories from your experience or a school deal/project: situation, your actions (specific tasks you did), concrete outcome with numbers. Keep each 60–90 seconds. (30–40 min)
- Walk through a quick 3-statement logic: an increase in revenue — how does it flow to EBITDA and to free cash flow? Say it aloud with numbers. (10 min)
- Valuation toolkit: explain DCF steps (project free cash flows, WACC, terminal value methods), multiples (EV/EBITDA, P/E) and when each is preferred; be ready to pick inputs and justify them. (20 min)
- One-minute story for “Why Lincoln?” and “Why investment banking/this shop?” (30–60 sec each). Tie to firm specifics (mid-market M&A focus, sector strengths, deal examples) — I can draft this once you give any firm notes. (10 min)
- Mock Q&A: practice 6 questions (below). Time yourself; answer out loud; I’ll score and fix any answer you type back. (30–40 min)
3) Core questions they will almost certainly ask (practice answers aloud)
- Walk me through your resume. (Structure: one-line current role, 2–3 relevant accomplishments, why it leads to banking.)
- Tell me about a deal or financial project you worked on. (Use S-T-A-R; include your modeling/analysis and impact.)
- How do you build a DCF? What are the main drivers? (Stepwise: forecast FCF, choose discount rate/WACC, pick terminal value, sensitivity)
- If company X has improving margins but negative free cash flow, what would you investigate? (Working capital, capex, one-offs, revenue quality)
- Walk me through an LBO at a high level. (Purchase with debt, projections, debt paydown, IRR drivers)
- A behavioral: tell me about a time you missed a deadline or had a conflict. (Focus on ownership, learning, outcome)

4) Quick technical drills (say these answers now)
- If revenue increases and gross margin is 30%, what is the impact on EBITDA and cash? (Walk through COGS, SG&A assumptions, taxes, working capital.)  
- How does an increase in depreciation affect free cash flow? (Up in non-cash expense lowers EBIT and taxes, but add back depreciation to CFO — net effect depends on tax shield and cash items.)  
- What’s the difference between enterprise value and equity value? (EV = value to all capital providers; add debt, subtract cash to go to equity value.)
5) Two short deal examples to have ready (templates — fill with your facts)
- Example A (M&A): "We [client/firm] considered [company], a [sector] business with [revenue]. I built [model or analysis], identified [value drivers], recommended [strategy], and the outcome was [result or next step]. I owned [specific tasks]."  
- Example B (project/analysis): "In [project], I detected [problem], ran [analysis], proposed [solution], which led to [quantified result]."
6) How I will help now (what I can do this turn)
- Run three mock questions and score your answers (I ask the first question now).  
- Or draft your "Why Lincoln" and "Walk me through your resume" lines if you paste 2–3 bullet achievements from your recent role.  
- Or produce a 10-point firm-specific prep sheet if you paste any Lincoln deal names or recruiter notes.

Next step (one question): Do you want to start a mock now (I’ll ask the first question), or paste 2–3 bullets from your current role so I can draft your resume walk-through and "Why Lincoln" answer?
